The Vampire Counts are fiends without equal. They seek to topple the civilisations of the living and supplant them with an Undead empire. Each Vampire is a unique and majestic figure with his own personality, drive and ambition. In contrast, their minions are mindlessly obedient - rank after rank of ragged and dirt-encrusted cadavers forced back to life by their masters' necromantic power.

The Empire of Man, the sprawling nation of humans dominating the Old World, faces a daily struggle for survival. Guided by their Emperor, Karl Franz, its armies stand as a testament to unwavering discipline and unmatched martial skills. In a world teeming with brutal savages and bloodthirsty monsters, the Empire endures thanks to the renowned discipline of its armies, honed through rigorous training and fortified by their unyielding faith in Sigmar. A beacon of human resilience, the Empire's soldiers exemplify the indomitable spirit of man that prevails amidst its endless list of foes.

The Kingdom of Bretonnia is a land renowned for powerful Knights and their strong sense of Chivalry. Guided by the Fey Enchantress and the Damsels of the Lady, the peasants toil while their noble lords protect them from the many dangers threating their survival. In times of war the whole kingdom can join together, led in a crusade against their enemies by King Louen Leoncoeur, against which no foe has known victory.

Mousillon, the accursed state nestled within the heart of Bretonnia, casts a dark and ominous shadow over the land. Once a proud dukedom, it now stands as a grim testament to the corruption that lingers in the shadows. Ruled by the Serpent of Mousillon, the realm of swamps and thickets contrasts against the vibrant setting of noble Bretonnia. Yet, even more tragic and unsettling are its mutated peasantry, ruled not by noble knights but the twisted undead, whose black knights evoke a chilling blend of traditional Bretonnian martial prowess and unholy power.

The Wood Elves are the elvish inhabitants of Athel Loren; they are a suspicious, isolationist and savage kin who live their lives surrounded by the nature of Athel Loren. Their magical forest home is as dangerous as it is beautiful, and its unforgiving nature has sharpened the skills of its people to a razor's edge. The Asrai live under the teachings of Isha and Kurnous as hunters and warriors defending the Weave and natural world, but darker voices ever seek to tempt them to slaughter and mayhem.

Between Nordland and the Wasteland lies the forest of Laurelorn and it's inhabitants, the proud Eonir. They refused to flee the Old World with the rest of their kin and instead stood against and defeated the dwarfish advance on their forest. The Eonir live in a caste society split between the city and forest kin, and maintain their security through careful diplomacy; both with their neighbours and factions as far abroad as the Asur and the Druchii. Their governance works through layers of councils to promote a level of democracy. When the time for battle comes Eonir call on everything from the darkest magic to the purest spirits of the forest to ensure the safety of their home.

The Dwarfs, or the Dawi in their tongue, are one of the oldest and proudest races of the world. The Everlasting Realm of the Dwarfs was at its peak when human nations were nothing more than bands of warring barbarian tribes. Hardy, stout hearts combined with, at times, excessive pride result in a harsh and durable folk – one that is utterly incapable of forgiveness. And so the Dawi record each and every single wrong suffered at the hands of other races, with hopes of avenging said grudges in the future. Alas, this merciless and stubborn attitude led the Dwarfs into a number of conflicts that eventually pushed their civilization into decline. Out of 22 major Dwarfen Holds, or Karaks, only 12 remain under Dawi control – with the remaining ones fallen into the hands of their Ancestral Foes: Skaven and Greenskins.

No one truly knows the origin of Chaos in the mortal world. Even the long-lived scholars of the High Elves can only speculate as to where the forces of Chaos first originated. War, famine, natural disaster and the destroyer known as time have eroded away nearly all indications of the roots of Chaos.

Orcs and Goblins have been a thorn in the side of every major and minor power for as long as anyone can remember. Caring nothing for history or legacy, in olden days the Greenskins were largely confined to the Southlands, where they waged savage wars amongst themselves, indifferent to the wider world. Yet this brutal isolation did not last. Earthquakes and volcanic activity drove them northwards in vast, rampaging hordes called Waaaghs!, looting and burning all in their path. The Dwarfs, weakened by the long and bitter War of Vengeance against the Elves, stood little chance against the green tide that washed over their homes, and many holds were lost. Ever since, Orcs and Goblins can be found in great numbers all over the planet, being outnumbered only by the Skaven, with whom they often wage wars deep underground.

The Cult of Sigmar, also sometimes called the Church of Sigmar, the Holy Temple of Sigmar, the Clergy of Sigmar or simply the Sigmarite Cult, is the state church of the Empire that administrates the worship of that realm's patron god, Sigmar Heldenhammer. The Cult of Sigmar was founded by the wild-eyed friar Johann Helstrum in the year 73 IC, when he appeared before the masses to relate a vision that he experienced of Sigmar kneeling before Ulric, the god of war and winter, who placed the crown of godhood upon his brow as Sigmar took his place amongst the deities of the Old World Pantheon. As of today, the Cult of Sigmar has become an essential part of Imperial society. Nearly every city, town or village within the Empire has dedicated a portion of their wealth and land to the creation and maintenance of a Sigmarite temple, from which a priest of the Cult of Sigmar will attend to the spiritual well-being of its citizenry, whether it be through holy words of prayer or through heroic actions and trials by combat.

The Cult of Taal and Rhya is among the most ancient and pervasive in the Old World, tracing a direct line to the primal gods from the deepest of history. The cult grew organically, as early Humans tried to explain natural phenomenon, such as thunder, the turning of the seasons, and the rise and ebb of the seas. Over time, the Gods Taal and Rhya came into being, beginning as a single entity, known as Ishnernos. This split occurred many thousands of years ago, and the Cult of Ishnernos faded into distant memory. Taal rules nature and is considered King of the Gods. He claims the wild places as his domain and is primarily worshipped by hardy woodsmen, trackers, and rangers. Rhya's worshippers are found in the cultivated fields and orchards of the Empire, as well as among farmers, fishermen, and young lovers everywhere. The Cult of Taal and Rhya is the sanctioned cult of Talabecland, and is wildly popular in the eastern and northern parts of the Empire. Of the two, Taal receives most recognition, and Rhya's role is much diminished. The grand city of Talabheim is particularly fervent in its worship of both Taal and Rhya. However, in other cities, although Rhya's name is commonly known, her worship is rare, leading many urbanites to conclude that her cult is on the decline.

The Ulrican cult, Church of Ulric or simply the Cult of Ulric is the state approved religious organisation that administrates the worship of the god of war, winter, and wolves. It is second in power and influence to the Cult of Sigmar, but is amongst the most ancient religions of the Empire of Man and dates back before the Empire was created by Sigmar. As a god of war, it is through battle and bloodshed that Ulric is worshipped, any who dare oppose him are merely awaiting the ferocious bite of his priests. {newline} {newline} Ulric give me the fangs of the wolf, {newline} Ulric give me the claws of the wolf, {newline} Ulric give me the coat of the wolf, {newline} And I will show your enemies the mercy of the wolf.

The Cult of Shallya is dedicated to the White Dove of Mercy, the Lady in White, Shallya. Compassion, mercy and healing are the doctrines of the cult, and her priests offer aid to those in need across the Empire. The Old World is a gruelling place filled with disease, injury and bad fortune that can drive a person to utter despair, it is these folk who turn to Shallya whose priests bring the promise of mercy and comfort. Her temples double as hospitals for those who cannot afford a physician, run by her devout priestesses for few men serve her order.

The religious organisation that oversees and administrates the worship of the god of the sea, oceans, and tides across the Old World. It is most prevalent along the western border of the Empire where the waters of the Sea of Claws touch the shores of man, and most influential within Marienburg. Its members are often navigators, pilots and able-bodied sailors and it is seen as immense luck to have a priest of Manann aboard your vessel. {newline} {newline} Manann be praised, for he is the breeze to take us out, {newline} Manann be praised, for he is the wave to bring us home, {newline} Manann be praised, for he is the food to feed us,{newline} Manann be praised, or his be the wrath that drowns us.

Myrmidia is the goddess of war and wisdom – One that is most popular in the southern realms of the Old World, such as Tilea and Estalia. Her providence inspires commanders with their unparalleled strategies and tactics, as well as soldiers, whose feints, blocks, and thrusts in combat almost seem like graceful and lethal choreography. Any combatant who fights with honour and for a just cause or one that seeks tactical knowledge will be favored by Myrmidia. Many would consider the Cult of Myrmidia to be the most organised religion in the Old World; the truth, however, is more complicated. There is a great deal of internal strife and contradictions within the Cult if one visits the great temple in Tilea and the Archecclesiastium in Estalia, each holding to their own beliefs, such as the legitimacy of Bellona Myrmidia and the Bellum Strategia. Tilean legends say that there was once a man called Tylos who made a pact with a goddess of wisdom and beauty and founded a great city with her help. However, Tylos wished his city to rival that of the elves, and in his hubris the city was doomed. Years later, when the elves left the Old World behind and humans slowly colonised the ruins, they found a newborn child in the ruins of what is now Remas. Her foster parents died young, and she was sold to a local duke infamous for his cruelty. Unable to bear his abuse any longer, the girl took up a spear and killed the duke. From then on she led Tilea and Estalia to greatness, with the aim to uphold the virtues of honour. Yet Estalians believe Myrmida to be the daughter of Morr and Verena, that she stepped forth from the heavens in Magritta, descending onto the same ground upon which the Archecclesiastium is built. In the bowels of the temple, pilgrims and priests alike can pray to the sacred rock with an imprint of Myrmidia's footprint.

The Cult of the Lady of the Lake, or simply the Cult of the Lady, is a state-official religious cult that serves to follow and uphold the values set upon them by the Lady of the Lake, and to serve the interest of her and the Kingdom of Bretonnia. Since ancient times, the Bretonnians have worshipped the Lady of the Lake as their goddess and their primary deity, a figure of myth and legend who guides their Kings and protects their lands from harm. Worship of the Lady can be traced to the earliest days of the Kingdom. It is said that she arose from a Sacred Lake before Gilles le Breton and his Knightly Companions on the dawn of the Great Victory of Bordeleaux. Wreathed in a fey light, the Lady rose from the water bearing a Grail which overflowed with light that spilled into the waters of the lake, blessing the assembled knights until dawn's light broke over the mountains.

Vampires of all kinds loathe the gods. They don't deny their existence, but they don't serve them, seeking to be their equal instead. The closest idea of a religion to vampires would be their shared recognition of Nagash as the creator of undeath. Ultimately, all vampires descend from him. Nagash, known by many names such as the 'Great Necromancer', the 'Great Betrayer', the 'Usurper', the 'Undying King', the 'Supreme Lord of Undeath' or simply 'He Who Shall Not Be Named' is the ultimate personification of death and the Undead, an ancient, evil being who sought to conquer this cruel, chaotic mortal world and bring about an age of Undeath that will rule for all eternity. Nagash is darkness and unreasoning hatred given form, the father and creator of the foul art of necromancy and lord of all Vampires. His every action and deed is self-serving, his achievement horrific and loathsome, and his every whim bent solely to ensure that no one shall ever deny nor challenge his right to rule ever again.

The term Chaos Undivided refers to a faction among the forces of Chaos that serves the pantheon of the major Chaos Gods as a whole rather than owing complete fealty to one over the others. It is often represented by the Everchosen of Chaos, the mortal Chaos Lord who is the greatest champion of all the major Chaos Gods. Followers of Chaos Undivided venerate the force of Chaos itself, sometimes as an entity that some insane scholars of the Old World name the 'Great Beast' in which the major Chaos Gods are seen as a single deity whose four major constituent parts are to be worshipped equally as different emanations of the same universal force. At times, this entity sets aside its mad internal struggle, which is otherwise known as the Great Game, to make it possible for the fragmented armies of the major Chaos Gods to gather together under one banner, such as during the various Chaos incursions into the Known World like the Great War Against Chaos and the End Times. These moments cause the Old World to tremble and quake in fear and loathing.

Slaanesh, also known as the 'Dark Prince', the 'Prince of Pleasure', the 'Lord of Excess', the 'God of Obsession', 'the Serpent', the 'Master of Excess in All Things', the 'Perfect Prince' and even the 'Prince of Chaos' is the major Chaos God of pleasure, passion, obsession, excess, hedonism, decadence and pain. Born of mortal inspiration and desire, Slaanesh is the great muse, the fulfiller of dreams. He is passion given form. He is pleasure incarnate, from the intellectual satisfaction of a problem solved to the fulfilment of baser desires. His is the domain of frustration and agony, the struggle to achieve that which mortals covet. He is titillation. He is suffering. He is the sum of all mortal experience.

Nurgle, also known as the 'Plague Lord', 'Grandfather Nurgle', the 'Lord of Pestilence', the 'Fly Lord', the 'Urfather' and 'the Crow' among many other names is the major Chaos God of disease, decay, despair, destruction, death and rebirth. Nurgle is the Chaos God most directly involved with the plight of mortals, particularly Men, who suffer so acutely from a fear of death. He is the eldest of the four Chaos Gods and indeed is undoubtedly the oldest Chaos God of all, for the process of death and decay is as ancient as life itself. Nurgle is the embodiment of the constant cycle of death and rebirth which animates all life in the universe, and was brought into being by mortals' fears of death and the despair they feel about their inevitable mortality from age and disease.

Khorne, also known as the 'Blood God', the 'Lord of Murder', the 'Lord of Skulls', 'Hunter of Souls' and 'the Hound' in Norsca, is the major Chaos God of war, hatred, wrath, rage, murder, blood, strength, courage and martial honour. Khorne is the second eldest of the major Ruinous Powers and his waxing strength in this time of constant conflict often renders him the mightiest of the Chaos Gods in his effect on the mortal world and in the Great Game between the gods. His domain encompasses the most basic and brutal of sentient emotions - hate, anger, rage, the desire for destruction and the joy of killing one's enemies. Every act of killing or murder in the mortal world feeds and empowers Khorne, the more senseless, vicious and bloodthirsty, the better.

Tzeentch, also known as the 'Changer of Ways', the 'Lord of Change', the 'Architect of Fate', the 'Wind-lord', the 'Raven God', and the 'Great Conspirator' is the major Chaos God of change, evolution, ambition, intrigue, destiny, lies, trickery, sorcery, knowledge, and mutation. Though weary scholars of daemonology know this god by the name of Tzeentch, in truth, he exceeds all the other Ruinous Powers in his number of facets, names and aspects. For he is change, said to embody every mortal creature's recognition of, and desire, to change, to grow, to move, to seek more -- more knowledge, more wealth, more power. His face and form shifts and turns from eternity unto eternity.

At the dawn of time, the first elves were born from Isha, and her place in their pantheon is appropriately prominent, behind only the creator of the world, Asuryan. She is especially important to the Asrai, as is her avatar, Ariel, the Queen-In-The-Wood. It is Isha who first taught the elves to care for the land, and in turn how the land would care for them. Isha is a goddess of life, first and foremost, and weeps at the death of any of her creations, but especially the deaths of her elven children -- it is said that when Asuryan decreed that the Elves would be long-lived, but not immortal, Isha saw their deaths and despaired; her anguish flowed out of her with such force that the tears became the inner sea of Ulthuan. Though direct contact with mortals is forbidden by Asuryan, even the god of wisdom’s attention is finite, and whenever his eye is elsewhere, Isha slips past to infuse the lands of the elves with her protective magic; and when she cannot act to protect her children herself, she petitions her daughter Lileath, the goddess of dreams, to send omens and portents that they might be forewarned of coming harm.

As Isha is the mother of the elven race, Kurnous, her husband, is the father. Kurnous the Hunter, Master of the Wild Places. He is of most importance to the Asrai, and his perennial avatar, Orion, is their King, reborn every spring by the hand of Ariel and the will of Kurnous. Kurnous’ sphere of concern is the hunt, and he has very specific opinions about how that hunt is to be done. His first commandment is to kill only those animals which you need to eat or who are lost to disease or madness. His second commandment is that Greenskins and Beastmen, or other chaos mutants, are to be driven from the forests and exterminated without pity. While his power is strongest in the ancient forests of the Asrai, especially Athel Loren and Laurelorn, he extends his will into all the wild places in the world, and woe betide those who disrespect his holdings.

Vaul is the elven god of smiths and artisans. In ancient days, when the gods warred among themselves, Vaul was defeated by Khaine, who blinded the smith and chained him to his anvil, where he labours to this day forging and maintaining the great artifacts of the elven gods. It is in his captivity by Khaine that he forged the greatest of the artifacts, the Widowmaker, for Khaine himself. In the forging of the Widowmaker. Vaul enlisted the aid of Draugnir, the father of Dragons, to temper the blade -- but the Widowmaker was, and is, a greedy weapon, and drew something of the essence of the great dragon into itself; and so the fate of elves and dragons was, and will be, forever entwined.

In many ways Anath Raema is defined by what she is not. She is a hunter, like Kurnous, but she cares nothing for the balance of nature. Hers is the chase and the kill, nothing more. Some, primarily among the Druchii, tell a story of Anath Raema courting Kurnous, and her rejection -- and worship her as a patron of jealous lovers, seeing their pursuit of the object of their affections as a facet of the chase.

The Creator God and Emperor of the Heavens, the oldest of the elven gods, rules the heavens and keeps the balance among gods and mortals from his throne in a great pyramid. Although he rarely speaks to his fellow gods and even less to the elves, it is said that every Phoenix King has come in contact with him. When a new Phoenix King ascends to the Phoenix Throne, he steps through the Flames of Asuryan, where the god himself touches the minds of the aspirant to judge his worth. Those deemed unworthy are burned by the flames, while the worthy are then reborn in the flames. So far, there has been only one that Asuryan rejected.

Loec, also known as the Shadow Dancer, is the elven god of laughter and tricks, a patron to all arts. As a part of the Cadai, the Gods of Heaven, Loec is usually portrayed as a benevolent deity, but as with all, he has a darker side. In this, he is the god of vengeance, shadows, and dark deeds as well. As such, he is said to dance among the void, stirring the souls that dwell there. With his nature of tricks and mischief, he is said to steal elven souls from the Chaos Gods, even if this saps his strength. The main worshippers of Loec are the Wardancers of the Wood Elves as well as the elves from the shattered lands of Nagarythe.

It is said that in the age when the Ancestor Gods still walked the world, the Dwarfen god Grimnir ventured northwards clad in nothing but his famed red crest and bearing his mighty axe. There, he met his doom, cutting down countless daemons until he reached the collapsed warpgate, where he stood vigil to bar their passage into the south. Since that time, those who now bear the name of 'Slayer' have followed in Grimnir's footsteps, seeking out mighty foes and striving to meet their end in battle or die trying. Yet it was in the time of King Baragor, the first of the Slayer Kings, that the Slayer Cult took a steep rise. Karak Kadrin became a haven for these doomed warriors, a place where they could find food and rest before marching towards their doom once more. The Cult of Grimnir is open to all warriors, but only a Slayer can access sacred shrines in Karak Kadrin. These deadly berserkers are bound by an oath to find their death against worthy foes, while regular warriors must uphold the warrior's code set by the cult, which includes attacking when possible, defending when required, always aiding your brothers-in-arms, and slaying as many foes as possible.

Valaya is the Ancestor Goddess of Home and Hearth, of Healing and of Brewing. She is responsible for the shaping of the Dwarfen culture, teaching her people the runic script known as Khazalid and instructing them in the art of brewing, for which the Dwarfs remain renowned to this day. It was also Valaya who bestowed upon her kin the arts of healing, a gift sorely needed during the first great incursion of Chaos. Whilst Grimnir ranged far in battle against the daemonic hosts, and Grungni laboured at the forge crafting weapons and armour, Valaya remained beside her people. She fought alongside them when needed and tended to the wounded when the battle was done. In the darkest days of the war, Valaya is said to have devised a mighty defensive rune, a warding barrier cast about the Dwarf holds. Any daemon that dared touch its power was banished back into the Realm of Chaos, unable to breach the sanctity of Dwarfen stone. When the war had passed and her teachings were complete, Valaya withdrew with the remaining Ancestor Gods, venturing deep into the mountains. Since that time she has not been seen, though her presence is felt in every hearthfire and every hold that stands unbroken against the dark.

In elder days, when the Ancestor Gods walked amongst the Dwarfs, foremost among them was Grungni, master of smithing and lord of the forge. Grungni foresaw the coming of Chaos and guided his people beneath the earth and into the safety of the mountains. There he taught them to shape metal into weapons and armour of peerless craft, preparing them for the darkness that was to come. When the hordes of Chaos descended upon the world, Grungni led his kin forth to war. Yet Chaos was not so easily cast down, and in time the Dwarfs were driven back to their mountain holds. Only Grimnir, brother to Grungni, dared to venture beyond the mountains to combat the enemy. Grungni remained behind, forging artefacts of immense power to aid his people. Among these was the Throne of Power, upon which was set the Rune of Azamar, the Eternity Rune, a rune so powerful only one has ever existed, and can never be replicated. It was Grungni’s only work where he felt satisfied upon its completion, and with the rune came a promise, for as long as the rune endures, the Karaz Ankor shall never fall. After the great war, the surviving Ancestor Gods withdrew deep into the mountains, awaiting the hour when their children would have need of them once more.

Little is known about the major greenskin gods, and for outsiders they are hard to differentiate. Gork and Mork, the twin gods, both share the attributes of being brutal and cunning, but for the greenskins, it is clear who to worship for which boons. Gork is the brutally cunning part of the twins, a god of raw strength and might. As such, his main worshippers are the orcs, who value strength above all. Shamans that beseech Gork will sometimes succeed in summoning the god himself, or at least part of him. If they should succeed, they can summon enormous grasping hands to pluck their enemies apart or gigantic feet to stomp the enemy forces. Such is the raw power of Gork.

Little is known about the major greenskin gods, and for outsiders they are hard to differentiate. Gork and Mork, the twin gods, both share the attributes of being brutal and cunning, but for the greenskins it is clear who to worship for which boons. Mork is the cunningly brutal of the two twins and is primarily worshipped by goblins and other smarter varieties of greenskin. While the way of Gork is simply punching someone in the face, the way of Mork is much more refined: a worshipper of Mork would try to distract their foe and then punch them in the back of their head. Shamans that invoke the power of Mork do so not only to still damage their foes but also to protect their own. They can petition their god to hold his protecting hands over other greenskins or to manifest the piercing gaze of the god himself in the shaman’s own eyes, obliterating everything in his line of sight with deadly rays of energy.

In life, Sigmar stood for the unification of Mankind, the destruction of evil and defiance against corruption. You hold the path set for you in his example high in your mind. To be a Priest of His faith is to be a Shepard to all mankind. Many of the cloth remain in their temples and cathedrals but you know the truth; the cursed and the damned must be sought out and vanquished.

To be a Wolf Priest is to be one of Ulrics champions, powerful, zealous, and blessed by the feral god himself. The battleground is where the word of Ulric is spread, and it is through bloodshed that he is honoured in worship.

Sired by Abhorash, the Blood Knight is a dark mockery of everything noble or virtuous that can be said about their mortal counterparts. Where before the Blood Kiss there was honour is now cruelty; faith turns to irreverence and duty falls to wanton ambition. This is true of all vampires but seems particularly tragic for the fallen knights of the Old World.

The von Carsteins have always been as ambitious as they are arrogant. With a history steeped in war, and intrigue, they consider themselves the true rulers of mankind, viewing mortals as little more than cattle. The von Carstein bloodline claims no single specialty in warfare or spellcraft; instead, they profess mastery over all such disciplines. To them, there is no art they cannot command, no foe they cannot outwit, and no weapon they cannot master.

To be a Man in the 25th century is to be one of thousands. The Old World finds itself on the precipice of destruction and turmoil, of chaos and death. No one in this age can be weak; some use the times to their advantage and turn warfare into wealth, combat into glory and tragedy into destiny. Mercenary they may call you, whatever the name no one will control your fate.

To be a knight of Bretonnia is to strive for the blessing of the Lady and her holy grail. Any man deemed worthy to sup from her chalice becomes a holy warrior honored and respected across all of Bretonnia and yet farther. The road to that goal is difficult, so much so that most knights fail to accomplish despite all sharing the same dream.

Damsels are sought out as children by the Fey Enchantress for their latent magical potential. Taken away from their families they are raised in secret to be potent guardians of fair Bretonnia. Upon completion of their training they embark out into the land, coming to the aid of the people and influencing knights in order to fulfill their martial potential.

While many of these dark magisters serve under immortal vampires, it is actually the study of death and undeath that predates the vampire. Necromancers dedicate their lives researching the ultimate question facing every mortal; how to live forever? To the philosophically virtuous necromancer, vampirism is but one of the more successful failures at answering this question. The true answer is believed by these fell scholars to lay in study and innovation of the work of Nagash, the first and greatest necromancer of all time.

Whether in the name of faith, purity or reward, Witch Hunters are charged with ending the threat created by all those who spread the taint of darkness. They justify their weapons, unconventional instruments and methods of investigations in the name of protecting innocent souls. A mostly thankless task, as even those who they are sworn to protect fear the shadow of a Witch Hunter at their threshold.

Foreboding and Dreadful, Knights of the Black Grail are the personal retinue of the mysterious Serpent of Mousillon. As strong as they are cunning, Knights of the Black Grail have a knack for strategy and show great aptitude when faced with the many politics of Bretonnia. Even so, their honeyed words and forked tongue often reach into the hearts of many, drawing more to their cause of "freeing" Bretonnia from the filthy lie of the Lady.

Amongst all the creations of Nagash, the Necrarchs are perhaps the closest in image to their dark lord. All Necrarchs are dedicated towards one single goal, furthering their necromantic power; hiding away from civilisation they endlessly study and practice their foul magic. On the few occasions one has left their self-imposed isolation, it is almost always followed by a trail of carnage and ruin as few can survive these eternal fiends.

Magisters of the Colleges of Magic lead a prestigious life as they are given space and resources to hone their skills in safety – all this in exchange for a life of service to their Order and the Empire as a whole. The duties of a Magister are vast and may range from the destruction of dark forces to advising the lords and ladies of the Empire in various matters. While ordinary men of the Empire may scoff at the necessity of Magisters, the wise know them to be wardens against Chaos and its sorcery.

Waywatchers serve as the ultimate watchmen of Athel Loren, lords over the many paths leading in and out of the ancient wood. Master woodsmen and hunters, they can lie in ambush for several days, fire unerringly accurate barrages of arrows, and lay terrifying traps designed to kill, maim and dishearten any trespasser. Few marksmen can even approach a Waywatcher’s ability with the bow, even among the elves, as these elves have drifted the furthest away from elven civilization, embracing fully the call of the living forest.

The Greylords were once powerful mages of Ulthuan, but they were exiled for their cruel experiments. Today, the Greylords continue their often-dangerous experiments in secret in Laurelorn, willingly teach their apprentices the forbidden magic. The Greylords are not to be trifled with, by their power alone has the forest of Laurelorn been saved many times, though some remain fearful their powers may also doom the Eonir.

Spellsingers have a unique bond with Athel Loren, they are bound to the forest through magical ritual, giving then the same communal awareness that dryads or treekin enjoy, without sacrificing their individuality. While the lesser Spellsingers commune with the forest, the greater ones can reshape it for building of homes or destruction of enemies. In Athel Loren Spellsingers are artists and mages, and invariably are the ones that travel outside the forest to engage in rare diplomacy. While both men and women become Spellsingers, the women typically become stronger due to Ariel's bond with the forest of Athel Loren.

The Old World is a home to numerous Knightly Orders. Their members ordinarily follow one particular deity, like the ferocious White Wolves of Ulric or the accomplished Blazing Suns of Myrmidia. But it's not uncommon to encounter secular Orders like the Knights Panther. While rather varied in terms of equipment, faiths, or beliefs, such knights ultimately share similar goals: promotion of their Orders and annihilation of all things foul. Knights of the Old World are also famous for their elite training, finest gear, as well as influence that extends across the four corners of the realm.

Fighting in the narrow underground tunnels is a tough and tedious experience. Equipped with the best gromril armor that the Clan can provide and in an impenetrable shieldwall formation, Ironbreakers are responsible for protecting the most vulnerable accesses of the karaks to the last breath. Serving as an Ironbreaker is considered a great honour, as only the strongest and bravest among the Dwarfs are admitted.

Dwarves are a proud race. Failure is an affront to their honor and a scar that is almost indelible. Dwarves whose honor has been tarnished become Slayers; they will abandon their family, their possessions, and even their clan to pursue a path of redemption. And there is only one way to redeem their honor: death in the battlefield. In times of war, slayers will abandon their self-imposed exile to put their martial skills to the service of the dwarven cause; where they will meet their final destiny.

All Elves comes to the defence of Athel Loren in times of need. Trained not only with bow, but also with spear, sword, mounted combat and in some cases magic, the Lords of the Glade herald in the might of the Wood Elves and the Spirits of Athel Loren. Leading the charge and conceiving battle plans like no other, these Lords and Ladies are great warriors on and off the field, out maneuvering and flanking with deadly strength.

The Dwarfs are masters of craft, their forge-fires burning with the memory of ages past. Among their greatest artisans stand the Runesmiths, proud descendants of Thungni, the Ancestor God of Runelore. Gifted with the sacred knowledge of Runecraft, they bind power into steel with secret glyphs passed down since the Time of Woes.{newline}{newline}Sworn to secrecy and perfection, a Runesmith's every blow upon the anvil echoes with meaning. Their armor is warded, their weapons etched with runes that can break sorcery or strengthen allies. Runesmiths are both warriors and artisans, unflinching defenders of Dwarfen tradition and honour.
